stem: Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) is:
options: the cash generated by operations before any payment to lenders, EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC
the dividends actually paid to shareholders during the year, as decided by the board
the cash available to shareholders after interest and net borrowing: NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt
net income after tax, taken from the income statement without any adjustments
explanation: FCFE is what shareholders could receive without hurting the business. It starts from NPAT (after interest), converts to cash with D&A, CAPEX and ΔWC, and adds net new borrowing. FCF (to the firm) is the pre-lender version; dividends are only what the board chooses to pay.

stem: Which of the following is the FCFE formula?
options: NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt
NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC − ΔDebt
NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC
EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt
explanation: Net borrowing brings cash IN, so ΔDebt is added (and a repayment, a negative ΔDebt, reduces FCFE). Dropping it is the missing-delta-debt error; starting from EBIT(1 − T) is the FCF formula.

stem: An analyst discounts forecast cash flows to shareholders, after interest and after net borrowing, at the cost of equity. The result is:
options: The equity value directly
Enterprise value (EV)
The value of the firm's debt
Book value of equity
explanation: FCFE is the cash for shareholders, so its PV at the cost of equity is the equity value. No EV − Debt + Cash step is needed.

stem: You want the equity value of a firm whose debt will rise and fall over the next five years. Which method fits best?
options: FCFE at the cost of equity, since it includes the planned borrowing and repayment
FCFF discounted at the cost of equity, since both are cash flows of the firm
FCFE discounted at the firm's overall rate, since the firm is what is being valued
The Gordon model with last year's FCFE as D1, since debt changes cancel out
explanation: FCFE already contains ΔDebt, so it values the equity cash flows directly at the equity rate. Discounting FCFE at the firm rate (a lower figure) is a rate mismatch; FCFF is a firm-level cash flow and needs the firm rate.

stem: How is FCFE related to FCF?
options: FCFE = FCF − (1 − T) × Interest + ΔDebt
FCFE = FCF + (1 − T) × Interest − ΔDebt
FCFE = FCF − Interest + ΔDebt, with interest before tax
FCFE = FCF, because interest is not a cash flow
explanation: Going from the whole firm to equity holders, subtract the lenders' after-tax interest (interest saves tax, so only (1 − T) × Interest is lost) and add net new debt. Using pre-tax interest ignores the tax shield on interest.

stem: Which of the following is NOT true of FCFE?
options: It is discounted at the firm's overall discount rate to give enterprise value
It can exceed net income when the firm is borrowing
It includes interest because it starts from NPAT
Its present value at the cost of equity is the equity value
explanation: FCFE is an equity-holder cash flow, discounted at the cost of equity to give equity. Enterprise value comes from discounting FCF at the firm's rate.

stem: Why is ΔDebt added in FCFE?
options: New borrowing brings cash in for shareholders; repayments (negative ΔDebt) take cash away
Debt is an asset of the firm, so more debt directly increases the value of equity
Interest is only paid on new debt, so ΔDebt measures the interest bill
ΔDebt converts the book value of equity into its market value
explanation: FCFE counts cash flows that equity holders can actually receive: operating cash after reinvestment, less what must go to lenders, plus new loans. If the firm repays $2 of principal, $2 less is available for shareholders.

stem: A firm's FCFE this year is much larger than its NPAT, mainly because of a large increase in debt. How should an analyst read that?
options: The firm has become more profitable, and the extra cash will recur each year
The firm should cut its dividends to match FCFE and keep the difference
NPAT must have been understated by the accountants in the income statement
A one-off boost from borrowing; capitalising it would overstate equity value
explanation: ΔDebt is cash from lenders, not earnings. A permanent perpetuity of FCFE that includes a big one-off ΔDebt overstates value; normalise borrowing before capitalising.

stem: A firm reports (in $ thousands): NPAT 420; D&A 90; CAPEX 150; increase in working capital 20; net new borrowing 60. What is its FCFE?
options: $280 thousand
$310 thousand
$340 thousand
$400 thousand
explanation: FCFE = NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt = 420 + 90 − 150 − 20 + 60 = 400. Leaving out net borrowing gives 340; subtracting it gives 280; forgetting the non-cash D&A add-back gives 310.

stem: A firm has FCF of $5.8 million, interest of $0.9 million, a tax rate of 30%, and repays $1.2 million of debt during the year. What is its FCFE? (in $ millions)
options: $3.70 million
$3.97 million
$5.17 million
$6.37 million
explanation: FCFE = FCF − (1 − T) × Interest + ΔDebt = 5.80 − 0.63 + (−1.20) = $3.97 million. Using pre-tax interest gives $3.70 million; treating the repayment as borrowing gives $6.37 million; omitting ΔDebt gives $5.17 million.

stem: Prairie Grain Co-op has (in $ millions): sales 9.0; cash operating costs 5.4; D&A 0.9; interest 0.45; tax rate 30%; CAPEX 1.1; ΔWC 0.2; net new borrowing 0.5. FCFE is expected to stay constant forever. The firm's overall discount rate is 8% and shareholders require 11% per annum. What is the equity value? (Answer in $ millions.)

steps.label: FCFE = NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt

solution: Equity = FCFE/R_E = 1.675/0.11 = $15.23 million (the 8% firm rate is not used for FCFE)

errors.label: Left out net new borrowing
errors.explain: New borrowing adds cash for shareholders and belongs in FCFE.

errors.label: Discounted FCFE at the firm's 8% rate
errors.explain: Equity cash flows carry the cost of equity (11%); 8% is the rate for FCF.

errors.label: Used FCF (before interest and borrowing) instead of FCFE
errors.explain: FCF is the whole-firm cash flow; shareholders get FCFE.

explanation: Income statement → NPAT → FCFE → equity at the cost of equity. Interest is deducted here (via NPAT), and net borrowing is added.

stem: Chinook Chemicals has EBIT of $6.0 million, a tax rate of 25%, D&A of $1.4 million, CAPEX of $2.0 million and ΔWC of $0.3 million. It pays interest of $0.8 million and repays $0.6 million of debt during the year. What is its FCFE? (Answer in $ millions.)

steps.label: FCF = EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC

errors.label: Subtracted pre-tax interest
errors.explain: Interest is tax-deductible, so the cost to shareholders is (1 − T) × Interest.

errors.label: Added the repayment instead of subtracting
errors.explain: A debt repayment is a negative ΔDebt and reduces FCFE.

errors.label: Left out ΔDebt
errors.explain: Net borrowing (here negative) must be added.

explanation: FCFE = FCF − (1 − T) × Interest + ΔDebt is the bridge between the two cash flows. Here the firm both pays interest and shrinks its debt, so shareholders receive $1.2 million less than FCF.

stem: Rideau Rail just generated FCFE of $4.2 million, expected to grow 4% per year forever. Shareholders require 10.5% per annum, the firm's overall discount rate is 8%, and there are 8.0 million shares. What is the equity value per share? (Answer in $.)

errors.label: Used FCFE0 in the numerator
errors.explain: The growing perpetuity needs next year's FCFE.

errors.label: Discounted at the firm's 8% rate
errors.explain: FCFE is an equity cash flow and takes the cost of equity.

errors.label: Forgot to divide by the number of shares
errors.explain: 67.20 is the total equity value in $ millions.

explanation: FCFE valuation is Gordon growth applied to cash flows to equity at R_E. Dividing by shares at the end gives the price per share.

stem: Okanagan Orchards has NPAT of $1.6 million, D&A of $0.7 million, CAPEX of $1.2 million and ΔWC of $0.15 million. It wants FCFE of $2.0 million to fund a special payout to shareholders. How much net new debt must it raise? (Answer in $ millions.)

steps.label: Required ΔDebt = target FCFE − FCFE before borrowing

errors.label: Subtracted in the wrong order
errors.explain: ΔDebt must make up the SHORTFALL: target minus what operations already provide.

errors.label: Added ΔWC instead of subtracting it
errors.explain: An increase in working capital ties up cash and reduces FCFE.

errors.label: Forgot to add back D&A
errors.explain: D&A is a non-cash charge in NPAT and is added back.

explanation: FCFE = NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt, rearranged for ΔDebt. Borrowing is the plug that closes the gap between operating cash and the payout target.

stem: In the course's notation, working capital (WC) is:
options: Cash + Inventory + Receivables − Payables, i.e. current assets − current liabilities
Inventory + Receivables only, because cash is not an operating asset
Cash + Inventory + Receivables + Payables, the sum of the current items
Long-term assets minus long-term debt on the balance sheet
explanation: WC = Cash + Inventory + Accounts Receivable − Accounts Payable = Current assets − Current liabilities. Payables are a liability, so they reduce WC. ΔWC is the CHANGE in this figure from one year to the next.

stem: A retailer builds up inventory before the holiday season and pays for it in cash. In the FCF formula this shows up as:
options: A negative ΔWC, which raises FCF
A positive ΔWC, which reduces FCF
Higher CAPEX, which reduces FCF
Higher D&A, which raises FCF
explanation: Inventory is part of WC, so more inventory means WC and ΔWC rise. A positive ΔWC is cash tied up in the business and is subtracted in FCF = EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC.

stem: A company's suppliers agree to wait 15 more days for payment. Holding everything else constant, what happens to ΔWC and FCF this year?
options: Payables rise, so ΔWC rises as well and FCF falls by the increase in payables
Payables rise, so ΔWC falls (is negative) and FCF rises by that amount
Nothing happens, because payables are not part of working capital in this course
Payables rise, so CAPEX falls and FCF rises by the amount of the increase
explanation: Payables are subtracted in WC. When they rise, WC falls and ΔWC < 0; subtracting a negative ΔWC in FCF adds cash. The firm is effectively borrowing from suppliers.

stem: How do the level of working capital (WC) and the change in working capital (ΔWC) differ in a free cash flow calculation?
options: WC enters FCF each year, and ΔWC is only a memo item with no effect on cash flow
ΔWC is the sum of cash and receivables, and WC is the sum of inventory and payables
WC is a level at a date; only the yearly change ΔWC = WC_end − WC_start enters FCF
They are the same thing because working capital is already a flow, not a level
explanation: FCF is a flow for one period, so it needs the change in WC over that period. Subtracting the whole WC level would charge the firm again every year for the same inventory and receivables.

stem: Which of the following would NOT cause a positive change in working capital (ΔWC > 0) in a year?
options: An increase in inventory
An increase in accounts receivable
An increase in the cash balance
An increase in accounts payable
explanation: Inventory, receivables and cash are positive items in WC, so an increase in any of them raises WC. Payables are subtracted, so higher payables lower WC. (The professor's list of positive ΔWC examples: inventory up, receivables up, payables down, cash up.)

stem: Why does an increase in inventory reduce free cash flow even though inventory is an asset the firm owns?
options: The firm paid cash for goods it has not yet sold, so cash is tied up
Inventory is a liability on the balance sheet, so it reduces cash flow
Inventory is expensed immediately for tax purposes, lowering cash flow
Inventory raises D&A, and D&A reduces FCF dollar for dollar
explanation: FCF counts cash, not assets. Buying inventory consumes cash now and returns it only when the goods are sold. The same logic applies to receivables (sales not yet collected).

stem: A mature manufacturer collects receivables faster and trims inventory, so its working capital falls by $2 million this year while EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX is $10 million. What is this year's FCF, and is it sustainable?
options: FCF = $12 million; the extra $2 million is a one-off release of working capital
FCF = $8 million, because ΔWC is subtracted as an outflow
FCF = $10 million, because working capital does not affect FCF
FCF = $12 million and the $2 million will recur every year
explanation: ΔWC = −2, so FCF = 10 − (−2) = $12 million. Releasing working capital is a one-time gain; capitalising it forever would overstate the firm's value.

stem: True or false: ΔWC equals working capital at the end of the year minus working capital at the start of the year, and a positive ΔWC reduces FCF.
options: True
False
explanation: True. ΔWC = WC_end − WC_start. FCF subtracts ΔWC, so cash tied up (ΔWC > 0) lowers FCF and cash released (ΔWC < 0) raises it.

stem: During the year a firm's inventory rises by 55, receivables fall by 20, payables fall by 15 and cash rises by 10 (all in $ thousands). What is ΔWC?
options: $30 thousand
$50 thousand
$60 thousand
$100 thousand
explanation: ΔWC = ΔCash + ΔInventory + ΔReceivables − ΔPayables = 10 + 55 + (−20) − (−15) = 60. A fall in payables RAISES WC. Treating the payables fall as a decrease gives 30; leaving out cash gives 50; treating the receivables fall as a rise gives 100.

stem: A firm's current assets rise from 612 to 655 and its current liabilities fall from 340 to 312 (in $ thousands). What is ΔWC?
options: -$28 thousand
$15 thousand
$71 thousand
$343 thousand
explanation: WC = current assets − current liabilities: 272 at the start, 343 at the end, so ΔWC = 343 − 272 = 71. Adding the change in liabilities instead of subtracting it gives 15; the ending level is 343; looking at liabilities alone gives −28.

stem: Foothills Robotics's balance sheet shows (in $ thousands) at the start and end of the year: cash 120 and 150; inventory 310 and 365; receivables 240 and 262; payables 205 and 248. What is ΔWC? (Answer in $ thousands.)
solution: ΔWC = 529 − 465 = 64 (positive: cash tied up, FCF falls by 64)

errors.label: Added the payables
errors.explain: Payables are subtracted in working capital.

errors.label: Left out cash
errors.explain: In the course's definition cash is part of WC.

errors.label: Reported the ending WC
errors.explain: The question asks for the change over the year.

explanation: Compute WC at both dates, then take the difference. Cash, inventory and receivables push WC up; payables pull it down.

stem: Kootenay Kayaks has EBIT of 410, a tax rate of 30%, D&A of 95 and CAPEX of 120 (all in $ thousands). Current assets rose from 840 to 905 and current liabilities rose from 515 to 598. What is its free cash flow? (Answer in $ thousands.)

steps.label: FCF = EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC

errors.label: Subtracted 18 instead of adding it back
errors.explain: ΔWC is negative (working capital fell), so subtracting it adds 18 to FCF.

errors.label: Left ΔWC out of the calculation
errors.explain: ΔWC belongs in FCF; here it releases 18 of cash.

errors.label: Subtracted the ending WC level
errors.explain: Only the CHANGE in WC enters FCF.

explanation: Liabilities grew faster than assets, so working capital fell: the business was financed partly by its suppliers and FCF is higher than the pre-WC figure.

stem: Gatineau Glass's annual cost of goods sold is $36.5 million. It negotiates to pay suppliers 10 days later, so payables rise by 10 days of cost of goods sold (use 365 days). By how much does this one-time change raise FCF this year? (Answer in $ millions.)

errors.label: Treated higher payables as an outflow
errors.explain: More payables lower WC, which raises FCF.

errors.label: Used 10% of COGS
errors.explain: 10 days is 10/365 of annual COGS (2.7%), not 10%.

errors.label: Counted the gain every year
errors.explain: The stretch is a one-off release, not a permanent annual gain.

explanation: Stretching payables is cash borrowed from suppliers: ΔWC falls and FCF rises once. It cannot be repeated each year unless terms are stretched again.

stem: Harbourfront Bakeries expects inventory to rise 40% from $1.25 million, receivables to rise 8% from $0.90 million, and payables to rise 15% from $0.60 million. Cash is unchanged. What is the expected ΔWC? (Answer in $ millions.)

errors.label: Added the payables increase
errors.explain: Payables are subtracted: more payables offset part of the inventory build.

errors.label: Counted inventory only
errors.explain: Receivables and payables also change.

errors.label: Used the ending levels instead of the changes
errors.explain: WC at the end is a level; ΔWC needs the differences.

explanation: Each item's change is level × growth rate. Inventory and receivables increase WC; the payables increase offsets part of it.

stem: The comparables approach to valuation:
options: discounts forecast dividends at the required return to obtain the price today
applies the multiple of similar firms (P/E, P/S, EV/EBITDA) to the target's earnings, sales or EBITDA
discounts free cash flows at the firm's overall discount rate to obtain EV
adds up the values of the firm's assets as if they were sold off in liquidation
explanation: Comparables need no forecast of future cash flows: price = benchmark multiple × the firm's own metric. The other three descriptions are the DDM, FCFF valuation and liquidation value.

stem: A regulated electric utility has paid steadily growing dividends for decades, and its payout policy is stable. Which method is the most natural way to value its shares?
options: Free cash flow to the firm, discounted at the cost of equity
Price/sales comparables, because dividends are not reliable
NPVGO, because the firm has no growth opportunities
The dividend discount model (Gordon growth)
explanation: Stable, predictable dividends are exactly the condition under which the DDM works well. FCFF discounted at the cost of equity mixes the wrong rate with a firm-level cash flow, and price/sales is a fallback for firms without earnings.

stem: Pathfinder Fibre pays no dividends and plans to borrow heavily to finance a network build-out over the next five years. You want the value of its shares directly from forecasts of what shareholders could receive. Which method fits?
options: FCFE discounted at the cost of equity
The Gordon growth model with D0 = 0
FCFF discounted at the cost of equity
A trailing P/E applied to this year's earnings
explanation: With no dividends the DDM has nothing to discount until payouts begin, and FCFE captures both the heavy reinvestment and the planned borrowing. FCFF would give enterprise value (and needs the firm's rate), and a trailing P/E ignores the build-out.

stem: A buyer wants the value of a target's operations regardless of how the target is currently financed, because it will refinance the target with its own mix of debt and equity after the takeover. Which approach fits best?
options: FCFE discounted at the cost of equity using current borrowing
The DDM using the target's current dividend and growth rate
The target's book value of equity from its balance sheet
FCFF at the firm's rate (EV), then Equity = EV − Debt + Cash
explanation: FCF is independent of the financing mix (it is before interest and debt flows), so it values the operations whatever the debt level. Equity is then derived from EV with the current net debt.

stem: How do FCFF and FCFE differ as valuation methods?
options: FCFF gives the value of equity, whereas FCFE gives the value of the whole firm
FCFF is discounted at the firm's rate to give EV; FCFE at the cost of equity to give equity directly
Both are discounted at the cost of equity, but FCFE is measured after taxes
FCFF is built from dividends, whereas FCFE is built from earnings
explanation: FCFF = EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC belongs to all capital providers (EV, firm rate). FCFE = NPAT + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC + ΔDebt belongs to shareholders (equity, cost of equity).

stem: A young software company has sales but negative earnings and pays no dividend. Peers trade at about 4 times sales. Which valuation is the most workable?
options: P/E comparables applied to this year's negative earnings per share
Price/sales comparables applied to the company's sales per share
The Gordon model using the dividend paid this year as D0
NPVGO using the no-growth value EPS1/R as the price
explanation: A P/E on negative earnings is meaningless and the Gordon model has no dividend to grow; a sales multiple still produces a positive number (SM 8-12 values a firm at 4.3 × sales per share).

stem: Why can the dividend discount model be a poor choice for a firm that retains most of its earnings?
options: Retained earnings are discounted at a higher rate than paid-out dividends are
The DDM cannot be used at all whenever ROE is above the required return
Firms that retain earnings have no required return on their shares
Dividends then say little about the cash the business generates, so they understate its value
explanation: The DDM values only cash paid out. If a firm reinvests most of its cash, current dividends are small or zero and say little about the value of the business; FCFE or FCFF capture the cash generated whether or not it is paid out.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a reason to prefer comparables over DCF methods?
options: They are quick and use observable market multiples
They avoid having to estimate a long-run growth rate and discount rate
They work for firms whose future cash flows are hard to forecast
Comparables require a detailed forecast of each future year's cash flows
explanation: Comparables rely on peers' multiples applied to current or next-year earnings, sales or EBITDA. The cost is the benchmark: peers must really have similar g, ROE and R (SM 8 CTQ 12). A detailed multi-year forecast is the DCF's demand, not comparables'.

stem: For a growing firm that pays no dividend, the DDM gives $22 per share while peers' P/E multiples imply $35. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: The peers' P/E multiples must be wrong, because the DDM is the more reliable method
The firm is certainly overvalued at $35, because the DDM value is lower
The DDM is likely unsuitable: tiny dividends hide the cash flows; cross-check with FCFE or FCFF
The two methods must always agree, so there must be an arithmetic mistake
explanation: When payouts are small, the DDM can understate value; the methods differ because their assumptions differ. A cash-flow model (FCFE/FCFF) fills the gap, and then you compare it with the comparables value.

stem: True or false: if you discount FCFF at the firm's discount rate, you must still subtract debt and add cash to reach the value of the shares.
options: True
False
explanation: True. FCFF discounted gives enterprise value. Equity = EV − Debt + Cash. By contrast, FCFE discounted at the cost of equity gives equity directly.

stem: To value a firm's operations independently of how they are financed, discount _____ at the firm's overall discount rate.
options: free cash flow to the firm (FCF)
free cash flow to equity (FCFE)
dividends per share
net income after tax
explanation: FCF is before payments to lenders and shareholders, so it is independent of the financing mix; its PV at the firm's rate is enterprise value.

stem: Two analysts value the same firm. One discounts FCF at the firm's rate and computes Equity = EV − Debt + Cash; the other discounts FCFE at the cost of equity. Their equity values differ. What is the most likely reason?
options: Their forecasts or rates are inconsistent; built consistently, the two methods should agree
FCFF always gives a higher answer than FCFE, so the gap is expected
The DDM must be used to break the tie, since it is the only exact method
FCFE should be discounted at the firm's rate to make the two agree
explanation: In theory both approaches describe the same business and should give the same equity value. A gap points to inconsistent assumptions, not to a rule that one method is higher. Discounting FCFE at the firm's rate would make a rate mismatch, not fix one.
